transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE); Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE); Tom Reynolds (Acme CTO); Aisha Khan (ML Eng); Julia Park (Infra); Ravi Sen (SRE)

Summary:
Quick edge-cases focused demo covering long context handling (30k+ tokens), high TPS (burst and sustained), streaming backpressure, client timeouts and Redwood's fallback/failover strategies. Customer wants predictable latency at 95/99, options for Dedicated and Private, and security/compliance attachments.

Topics:
- Long context and KV/prefix caching
- High TPS stress and autoscaling behavior
- Streaming backpressure, chunking, client timeouts
- Fallbacks: model variants, quantized paths, regional fallback
- Security: VPC / KMS / audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Laura: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Laura from Redwood. Miguel and I will walk through a short demo focused on edge cases you called out — long context, high TPS, and streaming weirdness.
[00:00:12] Tom: Yep, thanks. We're especially worried about tail latency when we push to, uh, 800–1,000 TPS and some of our prompts are 20–30k tokens, so curious how Redwood behaves.
[00:00:25] Miguel: Totally, great context. Quick agenda: we'll show Console metrics and Optimize recommendations, run a live API demo with a long context conversation, then simulate high TPS and show how backpressure is surfaced.
[00:00:38] Aisha: One ask — can you show what happens when we hit client-side timeouts? In our app some clients set 10s timeouts, others 30s.
[00:00:45] Miguel: We'll cover that. Also we'll show fallback routing — if a full-precision model is slower, we can route to a quantized variant or dedicated pool.
[00:00:55] Laura: Ok starting the Console — this is the per-route dashboard. You can see 95/99 latency, success rate, and token spend. For the demo we preloaded a long conversation — about 32k tokens — to exercise the KV cache.
[00:01:10] Miguel: (shares screen) On the left is Optimize suggestions; it recommends prefix caching for this route and a batching window of 20ms for typical latency/cost tradeoffs. Note: batching helps throughput but can add tail when bursts hit.
[00:01:30] Julia: Quick question — prefix caching, is that the same KV cache you mentioned in the notes?
[00:01:35] Miguel: Yes, KV cache — sometimes transcribed as K V cash, which is weird — basically we persist key/value for previous tokens so repeating context doesn't repeat compute. For very long contexts we do partial eviction to keep memory bounded, and we index by prefix hash so replays are quick.
[00:01:56] Ravi: How does that play with private deployments? We need keys to stay on-prem.
[00:02:01] Laura: On Private we let customers bind the cache store to your VPC and we support HSM/KMS for keying. We'll send the KMS integration notes after.
[00:02:12] Miguel: Demo API now: calling /v1/generate with model=redwood-llama-65b, context ~32k tokens, streaming enabled.
[00:02:20] (typing sounds)
[00:02:22] Miguel: Streaming chunks are emitted every ~200–400ms depending on token generation rate; Console shows per-chunk RTT.
[00:02:30] [00:02:30] (customer side: small crosstalk)
[00:02:35] Aisha: I see. If the client times out at 10s mid-stream, do you support resumable streams or do we lose the session?
[00:02:42] Miguel: Good question. By default if client disconnects we keep the KV cache for a short TTL so a reconnect within that TTL can resume with the same conversation ID. For stricter semantics we support a resume token flow — we can share the spec.
[00:02:57] Tom: And if we're doing 1k TPS sustained, how does Redwood avoid queuing that pushes 99th to 5–10s?
[00:03:04] Miguel: We have smart routing. For hosted customers we route by latency vs cost policy. If the hosted pool is overloaded we can route to Dedicated pools or a cheaper quantized variant. Autoscaling is reactive but also predictive with burst capacity. In the Console you can define SLOs that trigger additional capacity or fallback routing.
[00:03:25] Laura: Here's the stress tool — we're going to replay a 500 TPS sustained run then jump to 1,000 TPS burst to show backpressure. Note this is a demo env so numbers are illustrative.
[00:03:39] (demo script runs; sound of keys)
[00:03:45] [00:03:45] Miguel: You can see the 95 percentile climbs first, then the 99 spikes during the burst window. Console flags the backpressure and surfaces which model variant took on the traffic.
[00:03:58] Julia: Are these alarms integrated with Slack or PagerDuty? We need to tie to runbooks.
[00:04:02] Laura: Yes, we have alerting hooks — Slack, PagerDuty, webhook. You can also attach runbooks per alert.
[00:04:10] Aisha: About model variants — how seamless is the switch? Do we get semantic drift if we go from FP16 to an int8 quantized model?
[00:04:18] Miguel: There's risk. Optimize can run evals on your prompt set and report regression metrics. For high-risk prompts we recommend a canary rollout: 5% traffic to quantized variant, monitor perplexity / downstream metrics, and then expand. Also we support automatic fallback only for non-critical paths; you can opt in per-route.
[00:04:41] Tom: Timeouts — if we set a client-side 10s timeout and the system will route to a quantized model adding 200ms but the queue adds 9s, it's still risky. What's the best practice?
[00:04:52] Miguel: Two options: 1) use a shorter server-side SLO and let the SDK surface an explicit retry with fallback; 2) implement progressive responses — stream partial answers fast using a smaller context window while the heavier model finishes. We demo progressive streaming in a sec.
[00:05:06] (demo: progressive streaming with short prefix responses)
[00:05:15] Miguel: Notice the initial tokens stream quickly from a smaller footprint model; later tokens come from the heavier model. This reduces perceived latency.
[00:05:23] Aisha: Does progressive streaming change token accounting/pricing?
[00:05:26] Laura: Yes, you are billed for the models used per request — the Console shows blended cost and we surface per-token unit costs. Optimize can recommend when progressive streaming is cost-effective.
[00:05:36] Ravi: For Private/on-prem, how does autoscaling work if we have a fixed pool?
[00:05:40] Miguel: For Private we support reserved capacity with burst credits and policy-driven overflow to a preferred cloud region if allowed. Alternatively you can provision headroom and Redwood will recommend sizing based on historical load.
[00:05:55] Tom: Can you reproduce the client-visible timeout behavior? We'd like to see a 10s client timeout during a 1k TPS burst.
[00:06:01] Miguel: Yes — I'll switch the stresser to simulate client-side 10s timeouts on some connections. Running now.
[00:06:09] (stressing; metrics update)
[00:06:14] Miguel: We're seeing partial disconnects; Console shows session IDs with resume tokens and a short KV TTL. Some sessions reconnect and continue, some time out and error. The 99th is high for the affected window, and backpressure is evident as queued requests hit the routing threshold.
[00:06:32] Aisha: What about streaming chunk size? If chunks are too big, we see long pauses — can we control chunk frequency?
[00:06:38] Miguel: Yes, chunking is configurable per SDK: preferred chunk token size and flush interval. There's a tradeoff — smaller chunks increase overhead but reduce perceived latency. Optimize suggests chunk params based on your RTT distribution.
[00:06:51] Laura: To summarize technical capabilities: prefix/KV cache for long context, progressive streaming for perceived latency, fallback routing to quantized/dedicated pools, and per-route SLOs and autoscale config.
[00:07:05] Tom: That's helpful. Two final asks: run a reproduction of our 1k TPS burst with our prompt set and send logs; and share the security pack (SOC2 / ISO / KMS).
[00:07:15] Laura: We'll do that — Miguel will run the benchmark and attach logs; I'll send pricing and security docs.
[00:07:21] Miguel: One note — sometimes the transcript generator in these demos mangles product names, e.g., it might call our Optimize tool "Optimes" — disregard.
[00:07:29] (laughter)
[00:07:33] Laura: Ok, we'll circle back with dates for a technical deep dive and pilot contract. Thanks everyone.
[00:07:40] Tom: Thanks, that was great.

End transcript.
